title: BACE: Technical Skills & Applications - Technical Skills and Applications - Electrophoresis
subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA migrates toward the positive electrode (anode) because:
options: The phosphate backbone of DNA is negatively charged.
The deoxyribose sugar is positively charged.
DNA is hydrophobic and moves away from the buffer.
The nitrogenous bases are positively charged.
questions.explain: DNA is negatively charged at neutral pH due to the phosphate groups in its backbone, causing it to migrate toward the positive electrode.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: Which percentage of agarose gel is most appropriate for separating small DNA fragments (e.g., 50–200 bp)?
questions.explain: Higher percentage gels have smaller pore sizes, providing better resolution for smaller DNA fragments. 0.5-0.8% is used for very large fragments (>5kb).
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: What is the function of SDS (Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate) in SDS-PAGE protein electrophoresis?
options: It creates cross-links between proteins.
It denatures proteins and imparts a uniform negative charge relative to mass.
It stains the proteins for visualization.
It acts as a buffer to maintain pH.
questions.explain: SDS is an anionic detergent that denatures secondary and tertiary protein structures and coats the linear protein in negative charge, ensuring separation is based solely on molecular weight.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: When running a DNA gel, why is a 'DNA ladder' or 'marker' loaded into one lane?
options: To balance the electrical current across the gel.
To act as a negative control.
To provide reference bands of known molecular weights for sizing.
To verify that the ethidium bromide is working.
questions.explain: A DNA ladder contains fragments of known sizes (bp). By comparing sample bands to the ladder, one can estimate the size of the sample fragments.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: What is the primary difference between Native PAGE and SDS-PAGE?
options: Native PAGE separates proteins based on size, charge, and shape; SDS-PAGE based on size only.
Native PAGE uses agarose; SDS-PAGE uses polyacrylamide.
Native PAGE requires heating the sample; SDS-PAGE is run on ice.
Native PAGE is for DNA; SDS-PAGE is for proteins.
questions.explain: Native PAGE maintains the protein's folded structure and intrinsic charge, so migration depends on size, charge, and shape. SDS-PAGE denatures proteins so migration depends only on mass.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: You are preparing a 1% agarose gel in 50 mL of buffer. How much agarose powder should you weigh out?
questions.explain: 1% means 1 g per 100 mL. For 50 mL, you need $0.5 \times 1\text{ g} = 0.5\text{ g}$.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: Which dye is commonly added to the DNA sample loading buffer (not the gel stain) to track migration progress visually?
options: Ethidium Bromide
Bromophenol Blue
SYBR Safe
Coomassie Blue
questions.explain: Bromophenol Blue (and Xylene Cyanol) are tracking dyes added to the sample buffer. They migrate at specific rates, allowing the user to see how far the electrophoresis has progressed.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: What happens if you accidentally swap the leads (red and black) when connecting the power supply for a DNA gel?
options: The gel will melt immediately.
The DNA will migrate out of the wells into the buffer tank instead of down the gel.
The DNA will migrate faster than normal.
The bands will be wavy and distorted.
questions.explain: DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the red (positive) electrode. If leads are swapped, the wells (at the top) are near the positive electrode, so DNA runs 'backwards' out of the gel.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: In Western Blotting, which follows SDS-PAGE, what is the purpose of the 'transfer' step?
options: To move proteins from the gel onto a solid membrane (e.g., nitrocellulose).
To stain the proteins with Coomassie Blue.
To denature the proteins further.
To wash away the SDS.
questions.explain: The transfer step moves the separated proteins from the fragile gel matrix onto a membrane (PVDF or Nitrocellulose) where they are accessible for antibody binding.
questions.subject: Technical Skills and Applications

questions.q: Why is Polyacrylamide generally preferred over Agarose for separating proteins?
options: It is non-toxic compared to agarose.
It has a much smaller pore size, suitable for resolving smaller molecules like proteins.
It does not require a buffer.
It can be run horizontally.
questions.explain: Polyacrylamide forms a tighter mesh (smaller pores) than agarose, making it suitable for resolving proteins (kDa) and very small DNA fragments, whereas agarose is better for larger DNA (kb).
